lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Gustavo Marinho de Carvalho | Lesson 10 -- Enjoy Doing, Decide to Do

listenings.text: There is a moment in learning anything as an adult that almost nobody warns you about, and it arrives at the worst possible time. For the first few months everything you learn is visible. You could not say a thing on Monday and by Friday you can, and the line on the graph goes up in a way you can feel. Then it stops. Not because you have stopped improving, but because what improves next is invisible from the inside: the same sentence, half a second faster. The same idea, with one fewer pause in the middle. Nobody can see that from where you are standing, and it feels exactly like standing still. That is where most people give up, and it is the single worst place to stop, because everything on the other side of it is the part that actually sounds like fluency.

A colleague of mine studied on her own for about a year, and she was disciplined about it in a way I never managed. Every morning, forty minutes, before anybody else was awake. Vocabulary lists, grammar exercises, a podcast on the way to work. And after a year she could read almost anything and she still could not hold a conversation for five minutes. So she changed one thing, and only one. She kept everything she was doing and added two conversations a week with a person who let her finish her own sentences. Six weeks later the difference was so obvious that people asked her what course she had taken. She had not taken any course. She had simply noticed that she had spent a year practising the thing she was already good at, which is what almost everybody does when nobody is watching.

paras: The story everybody knows is that children learn languages easily and adults do not. Part of that is true, and the true part is not the part people usually mean. Adults are worse at two specific things: sounding like a native speaker, and tolerating being bad at something in public. Neither of those is about the brain.

What adults are better at is almost everything else. They already know how a language works, so they do not have to discover the idea of a tense. They can read, which doubles the amount of input available in a week. And they can study a pattern in ten minutes that a child absorbs over ten months, because the child is not allowed to be told.

The variable that actually predicts progress is not age at all. It is the number of minutes an adult spends speaking each week, and whether those minutes are spent with somebody who lets them finish a sentence. Everything else -- the app, the book, the method -- moves that number or it does not, and if it does not, it is a hobby rather than a plan.

And then there is the part nobody mentions. After the first few months progress stops being visible, because what improves next is speed rather than range. The same sentence, half a second faster, with one fewer pause in the middle. From the inside that feels exactly like standing still, and it is where most people decide to give up. It is also the point after which everything sounds like fluency.
reading.source: Written for this lesson. The claims are general and reflect what is widely reported about adult language learning.
